lesson.title: When Once Isn't Enough: Applying L'Hopital's Rule Again and Again
lesson.summary: Sometimes differentiating the top and bottom of a limit once still leaves you with 0/0 or infinity/infinity. When that happens, L'Hopital's Rule can legally be applied again, and again, for as many rounds as the indeterminate form persists.
lesson.body:
L'Hopital's Rule says that if the limit of f(x)/g(x) is an indeterminate 0/0 or infinity/infinity form, then that limit equals the limit of f'(x)/g'(x), provided the second limit exists. Nothing in that statement guarantees the new quotient f'(x)/g'(x) will actually be easy to evaluate. If plugging in the limit point still produces 0/0 or infinity/infinity, you have simply produced a new indeterminate limit, and you are allowed to apply the rule to it again: differentiate the current numerator and denominator once more and check the form again. There is no fixed number of times you are allowed to do this; you repeat the process for exactly as many rounds as the indeterminate form keeps showing up, and you stop the moment substitution gives a real, determinate number, or the rule's other conditions stop holding, at which point a different method is needed.

The one rule you must never skip is rechecking the form before each new application. L'Hopital's Rule only applies to 0/0 or infinity/infinity. If you differentiate a numerator and denominator that are no longer indeterminate at the limit point, and divide the new derivatives anyway out of habit, the result can be completely wrong. Each round is really a fresh, independent application of the same theorem to a new pair of functions, f'(x) and g'(x), which just happen to have come from differentiating the previous pair.

Consider the limit as x approaches 0 of (x - sin x) / x^3, a limit that shows up when comparing how fast x and sin x pull apart near the origin. Plugging in x = 0 gives (0 - sin 0)/0^3 = 0/0, so L'Hopital's Rule applies. Differentiating top and bottom: the numerator's derivative is 1 - cos x, and the denominator's derivative is 3x^2. At x = 0 this gives (1 - cos 0)/(3 times 0^2) = (1-1)/0 = 0/0 again, still indeterminate, so apply the rule a second time. Differentiating again: the numerator's derivative is sin x, and the denominator's derivative is 6x. At x = 0 this is sin(0)/(6 times 0) = 0/0 once more. Apply the rule a third time: the numerator's derivative is cos x, and the denominator's derivative is 6, a constant. Now at x = 0, cos(0)/6 = 1/6, a real number with no zero in the denominator, so the chain stops here. Tracing back through all three applications, the limit as x approaches 0 of (x - sin x)/x^3 equals 1/6.

Notice how each round used exactly the same justification as a single L'Hopital step: confirm the indeterminate form, differentiate numerator and denominator separately, never as a quotient, which would be the quotient rule and a completely different operation, and evaluate again. Three quiet applications of one rule solved a limit that no amount of ordinary algebraic simplification handles as cleanly.
